case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a student who has settled an IDEA administrative complaint must still exhaust IDEA procedures under 20 U.S.C. § 1415(l) before bringing an ADA (and related state-law disability) lawsuit seeking compensatory damages that IDEA cannot provide.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 20 U.S.C. § 1415(l) (IDEA exhaustion provision); related substantive claims arise under the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.) and, in the lower courts, Michigan’s Persons with Disabilities Civil Rights Act.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Perez argues that § 1415(l) requires exhaustion only when a plaintiff is seeking relief that is actually available under the IDEA. Because his ADA suit seeks compensatory damages—a remedy not available in IDEA administrative proceedings—there is no IDEA “relief” to exhaust, and requiring exhaustion after his IDEA matter was settled would be pointless and inconsistent with the statute’s text, history, and the Court’s gravamen-focused approach in Fry.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Sturgis Public Schools argues that Perez’s ADA and state-law claims are, in substance, about denial of a free appropriate public education (FAPE) and therefore fall within IDEA’s exhaustion rule. Even if Perez labels the case as seeking damages, the gravamen of the complaint overlaps with IDEA-type educational harms, so § 1415(l) should bar the ADA suit unless IDEA procedures were fully exhausted (and settlement should not automatically eliminate the exhaustion requirement).
key_precedents: Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools, 137 S. Ct. 743 (2017)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ctr. for Bio-Ethical Reform, Inc. v. Napolitano, 648 F.3d 365 (6th Cir. 2011)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest argument remains the artful-pleading concern: that damages claims will be used to bypass IDEA’s expert FAPE process. But § 1415(l) makes exhaustion turn on whether the plaintiff is “seeking relief that is also available” under IDEA, and as Justice Barrett stresses, rewriting that remedial trigger into a categorical “FAPE-related harm” trigger effectively deletes the limiting words Congress chose. Justice Kagan’s point is also persuasive that Fry’s gravamen framework presupposes we still honor the statute’s “also available” limitation; when the only remedy sought is compensatory damages, the administrative process cannot award it, so further exhaustion becomes an empty formality rather than a meaningful channeling device. A narrow holding limited to damages-only (or otherwise IDEA-unavailable) remedies answers the statutory question without destabilizing the broader exhaustion regime, preserving institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument—that plaintiffs will plead around IDEA by styling FAPE disputes as ADA damages claims—cannot override the textual trigger Congress enacted: exhaustion is required only when the action is “seeking relief that is also available” under the IDEA, and compensatory damages are not available there. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the Sixth Circuit’s approach effectively treats “relief” as the underlying “wrong,” which reads the limiting words “also available” out of §1415(l) and converts it into a categorical FAPE-related exhaustion rule. Justice Barrett is also right that Fry’s gravamen inquiry does not authorize deleting the remedy-availability condition; it is a tool for identifying what the suit seeks, not for expanding administrative exhaustion beyond the agency’s remedial power. Requiring additional exhaustion after an IDEA settlement, when the only requested remedy is damages, would impose a judge-made procedural barrier untethered to any obtainable IDEA relief and thus conflicts with original public meaning and the statute’s text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the risk of artful pleading that would let ADA damages claims function as an end-run around IDEA’s expertise in FAPE disputes. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 1415(l) makes exhaustion turn on the “relief” sought being “also available” under IDEA, and compensatory damages are not within the administrative tribunal’s remedial power—so a harm-based rule effectively rewrites “relief” to mean “wrong.” Practically, requiring further exhaustion after an IDEA settlement, when the only remaining request is money damages, is empty formality and would perversely discourage settlements, a consequence Congress did not clearly command in the statutory text. Fry’s gravamen inquiry can help identify when a plaintiff is really seeking IDEA-type remedies, but it cannot erase the statute’s remedy-availability limitation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument is that ADA damages claims can be used to evade IDEA’s expert, FAPE-focused administrative process, but § 1415(l) ties exhaustion to the availability of the *relief* the plaintiff seeks—not merely to whether the facts involve a FAPE dispute—and damages are not obtainable through IDEA procedures. Justice Kagan and Justice Roberts correctly emphasize that Fry’s gravamen inquiry cannot be weaponized to erase Congress’s limiting phrase “seeking relief that is also available under” the IDEA; otherwise “relief” would effectively mean “wrong,” collapsing the statute into a categorical FAPE-related exhaustion rule Fry rejected. Requiring continued exhaustion after an IDEA settlement would be a hollow procedural obstacle that delays accountability and, in practice, burdens disabled students and families least able to endure protracted process. I therefore remain with petitioner: when the only requested remedy is compensatory damages unavailable under IDEA, § 1415(l) does not bar the ADA action.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the institutional one—IDEA expertise and fact development in FAPE disputes—but § 1415(l) makes exhaustion turn on whether the civil action is “seeking relief that is also available” under IDEA, not on whether the underlying harm is FAPE-related. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, the Sixth Circuit’s harm-based approach effectively rewrites “relief” to mean “wrong,” which deletes Congress’s limiting words and cannot be justified by Fry’s gravamen inquiry. Justice Barrett’s observation that Fry reserved the damages question matters, but the reservation cuts against importing a categorical FAPE exhaustion rule: Fry repeatedly ties exhaustion to what is “available,” and compensatory damages are not. Pragmatically, requiring post-settlement administrative steps when the agency cannot award the only remedy sought is an empty formality that undermines statutory coherence rather than advancing it.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point—pressed as an anti–artful pleading concern—is that any FAPE-gravamen claim should be routed through IDEA procedures first, but that substitutes a policy preference for Congress’s textual trigger: an action “seeking relief that is also available” under the IDEA. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, Fry’s gravamen inquiry cannot be used to delete the limiting words “also available” and convert § 1415(l) into a categorical FAPE-related exhaustion mandate; “relief” ordinarily denotes remedies, and compensatory damages are not within the IDEA’s administrative remedial authority. Justice Alito’s practical point reinforces the text: requiring families to prolong or forgo IDEA settlements just to preserve an ADA damages claim would create an extra-statutory obstacle with no corresponding administrative remedy to exhaust. On this record—damages-only after an IDEA settlement—there is nothing IDEA can still provide, so imposing exhaustion would be a judge-made prerequisite inconsistent with separation-of-powers principles.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best argument remains that exhaustion should attach whenever the underlying injury is a denial of FAPE, so the IDEA process can develop facts and apply expertise. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, § 1415(l) makes exhaustion turn on whether the plaintiff is “seeking relief that is also available” under the IDEA, and compensatory damages are not available in IDEA administrative proceedings—so requiring further “exhaustion” would be an empty formality not grounded in the statutory text. Fry’s gravamen inquiry helps identify when a suit is functionally about FAPE, but it does not authorize rewriting Congress’s remedial trigger into a categorical subject-matter bar. Practically, as Justice Alito notes, a harm-based rule would pressure families to avoid or delay IDEA settlements just to preserve ADA damages claims, an implausible regime absent clear congressional instruction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument is that exhaustion should turn on whether the injury is FAPE-related (so the agency can develop facts and apply expertise) regardless of the remedy requested, but that reading cannot be squared with § 1415(l)’s text conditioning exhaustion on “seeking relief that is also available” under the IDEA—i.e., remedy-availability, not mere subject-matter overlap. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, the Sixth Circuit’s approach effectively reads “relief” out of the statute and replaces it with a freestanding “harm” trigger, which Fry’s gravamen inquiry does not authorize; Fry reserved the damages question and repeatedly tied exhaustion to what the suit “seeks” and what is “available.” Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers point reinforces that courts should not expand exhaustion beyond Congress’s expressed condition, especially where the IDEA process cannot award compensatory damages and the prior IDEA proceeding was settled, making further exhaustion an empty formality. I therefore remain convinced that a damages-only ADA suit does not trigger § 1415(l).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the anti–artful pleading concern—i.e., that ADA damages claims will routinely be used to bypass IDEA expertise whenever the underlying dispute is FAPE-related—but that argument cannot overcome §1415(l)’s textual trigger: exhaustion applies only when the plaintiff is “seeking relief that is also available” under IDEA. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan stress, Fry’s gravamen framework asks what the suit seeks to obtain, and it does not authorize converting “relief” into “injury” in a way that erases Congress’s limiting words. Justice Alito’s practical point reinforces my procedural-fairness concerns: a rule requiring additional, remedially futile exhaustion would pressure families to prolong or reject IDEA settlements simply to preserve separate ADA damages claims, an inefficient and inequitable consequence absent clear statutory command. Even crediting the agency-expertise rationale, where compensatory damages are unavailable and the IDEA proceeding has already resolved forward-looking educational remedies, further exhaustion becomes an empty formality rather than a meaningful procedural safeguard.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1415(l) by its terms requires exhaustion only when the civil action is “seeking relief that is also available” under the IDEA; compensatory damages are not available in IDEA administrative proceedings, so there is no IDEA relief to exhaust. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools instructs that the exhaustion inquiry turns on what the lawsuit in fact “seeks,” not what it could have sought, and the Sixth Circuit’s harm-only approach reads the word “relief” out of the statute. Requiring further IDEA exhaustion after an IDEA complaint has been settled would impose a procedural hurdle without corresponding remedial payoff, undermining the statute’s narrow exhaustion mandate and inviting unnecessary litigation over process rather than merits. A narrow holding limited to suits seeking damages unavailable under IDEA respects the statutory text and preserves institutional legitimacy while leaving IDEA exhaustion in place when plaintiffs seek IDEA-type remedies.

Reading “relief” according to its ordinary meaning, the provision turns on remedy-availability, not merely whether the underlying facts relate to a denial of FAPE, and requiring further exhaustion after a settlement would impose procedures untethered to any IDEA relief the agency could grant. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools directs courts to identify when a suit is, in substance, about FAPE, but it does not justify expanding § 1415(l)’s exhaustion requirement beyond what the statute’s text covers. Because Perez’s ADA suit seeks a form of relief unavailable under the IDEA, § 1415(l) does not bar it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1415(l) by its terms requires exhaustion only when a plaintiff brings a non-IDEA action "seeking relief that is also available" under the IDEA; compensatory damages are not available in IDEA administrative proceedings, so the statutory trigger is not met. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools instructs courts to focus on the substance of what the plaintiff is seeking, and where the requested remedy cannot be obtained through IDEA procedures, insisting on further exhaustion after an IDEA settlement would be an empty formality with no practical payoff. Although the underlying wrong may involve a FAPE-like dispute, the text Congress chose in § 1415(l) ties exhaustion to the availability of the relief, not merely to overlap in subject matter. Requiring children to refuse settlements to preserve distinct ADA damages claims would impose impractical consequences not supported by the statute’s language.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1415(l) requires exhaustion only for a “civil action … seeking relief that is also available under” the IDEA, and compensatory damages are not relief the IDEA administrative process can “obtain,” so there is nothing meaningful to exhaust. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools directs courts to look to the substance of the complaint, but it also emphasized that “available” means relief that is “accessible or may be obtained,” leaving open (but strongly implying) that exhaustion is not required when the only relief sought is unavailable in IDEA proceedings. Requiring further exhaustion after an IDEA settlement would be a hollow procedural barrier that delays accountability and disproportionately burdens students with disabilities seeking full redress under the ADA. The better reading, consistent with Fry’s text-focused approach and Congress’s limits in § 1415(l), is that Perez’s ADA damages action may proceed without additional IDEA exhaustion.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1415(l) triggers exhaustion only when a plaintiff seeks “relief that is also available under” the IDEA, and compensatory damages are not available in IDEA administrative proceedings, so there is nothing to exhaust once the requested remedy lies outside IDEA’s remedial scheme. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools directs courts to focus on the kind of relief sought, not merely whether the underlying facts relate to a denial of FAPE, and that framework fits a damages-only ADA suit even if the educational injury overlaps with IDEA concerns. Requiring further exhaustion after the parties settled the IDEA complaint would be unworkable and inconsistent with the statute’s text, which is written as a remedial-availability gate rather than a categorical “FAPE-related” bar. This reading also preserves statutory coherence by allowing IDEA’s expert, forward-looking procedures to operate where they can provide relief, while leaving damages claims to the ADA and related statutes as Congress anticipated in § 1415(l).

Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools confirms that § 1415(l) limits exhaustion to circumstances where the relief sought is IDEA-available, and it treats the exhaustion inquiry as turning on what the suit seeks to obtain rather than imposing a free-floating FAPE-based bar. Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1415(l) by its terms requires exhaustion only when a plaintiff’s ADA (or other non-IDEA) action “seek[s] relief that is also available under” the IDEA, and compensatory damages are not relief available in IDEA administrative proceedings. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools instructs courts to focus on the gravamen of the complaint and the relief sought; when the suit seeks a remedy outside IDEA’s remedial scheme, the statutory trigger for exhaustion is not met. Requiring further exhaustion after an IDEA administrative matter has been settled would be impractical and unworkable—forcing families to forgo timely educational settlements merely to preserve distinct ADA damages claims—and would extend exhaustion beyond the statute’s text. Consistent with judicial restraint and respect for Congress’s design, the exhaustion requirement should not be expanded to bar an ADA damages suit where IDEA procedures cannot provide the requested remedy.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1415(l) requires exhaustion only for “a civil action…seeking relief that is also available under” the IDEA; on its ordinary meaning, that condition is not met when the plaintiff seeks compensatory damages, a form of relief IDEA administrative procedures cannot award. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools instructs courts to look to the gravamen of the complaint to determine whether the suit is, in substance, for the denial of a FAPE, but it also emphasized that § 1415(l)’s trigger is the relief sought and expressly reserved the damages question. Because the IDEA proceeding here was settled and the subsequent ADA suit seeks only remedies unavailable under IDEA, exhaustion is not required.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1415(l) requires exhaustion only for a “civil action…seeking relief that is also available under” the IDEA, and compensatory damages are not a remedy IDEA administrative procedures can award. Napoleon Community Schools, the exhaustion inquiry focuses on the gravamen of the complaint and—critically here—the statute’s text limits exhaustion to cases seeking IDEA-available remedies, so requiring further IDEA process after an IDEA settlement would be procedurally pointless and inconsistent with the ordinary meaning of “available.” Reading “relief” to mean merely “a wrong” rather than “a remedy,” as the respondent urges, would effectively erase Congress’s “also available under” limitation and impose burdensome process without practical benefit. This construction better serves procedural fairness and ensures that students are not trapped in administrative proceedings that cannot provide the compensation they seek under the ADA.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 20 U.S.C. § 1415(l) requires exhaustion only for an “action . . . seeking relief that is also available under” the IDEA, so where a plaintiff seeks solely compensatory damages—a remedy the IDEA does not provide—the exhaustion condition is not met. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools instructs courts to look to the gravamen of the complaint to determine whether the suit seeks IDEA-type relief for denial of a FAPE, but it expressly reserved whether exhaustion applies when the only relief sought is damages unavailable under the IDEA. Reading § 1415(l) according to its ordinary meaning and consistent with Fry’s framework, a damages-only ADA claim is not “seeking relief” available under the IDEA, even if the underlying facts involve educational services. Requiring exhaustion here would expand § 1415(l) beyond its textual limitation and effectively make the IDEA’s administrative process a prerequisite for remedies Congress did not place within that scheme.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1415(l) requires IDEA exhaustion only for suits "seeking relief that is also available" under the IDEA, and compensatory damages for disability discrimination are not an IDEA remedy; forcing exhaustion in that circumstance would read the statute’s remedial limitation out of the text and perversely block ADA claims even after an IDEA matter has been resolved by settlement. Fry v. Napoleon Community Schools directs courts to ask whether the gravamen is denial of a FAPE, but even when the dispute is education-related, § 1415(l) still turns on the relief sought—here, damages the IDEA cannot provide—so additional administrative process would serve no practical remedial function. Interpreting exhaustion to bar non-IDEA remedies would undercut Congress’s purpose in § 1415(l) of preserving parallel enforcement of federal disability-rights statutes and would impose unnecessary procedural hurdles on students with disabilities without advancing procedural fairness. Accordingly, Perez’s ADA and parallel state-law damages claims should be allowed to proceed without further IDEA exhaustion once IDEA proceedings have concluded.
